items.stem: Which term matches this description: "One of the broad fields of the SCA course, such as Classifying the world, Health, illness and healing, Social and cultural organization, or Movement, time and space"?
options: area of inquiry
command term
comparative essay
self-assessment
items.answer: area of inquiry
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of area of inquiry.

items.stem: Briefly explain why candidates should link their ethnography explicitly to the area of inquiry and key concepts.
items.answer: The question tests understanding of the area of inquiry; making links explicit shows how the ethnography illuminates the concept rather than leaving the examiner to infer relevance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The question tests understanding of the area of inquiry; making links explicit shows how the ethnography illuminates the concept rather than leaving the examiner to infer relevance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The more ethnographies an answer mentions, the higher its mark." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Markbands reward depth, accuracy and analysis; many brief references usually signal superficial knowledge.
items.markingKey: Markbands reward depth, accuracy and analysis; many brief references usually signal superficial knowledge. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Draft introduction by a student: "In this essay I will discuss how migration changes identity. Holmes (2013) studied Triqui migrant farmworkers from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and California in 2003–2005, using participant observation as a picker. I will argue that migration does not simply change identity but places migrants into an ethnic-citizenship hierarchy that is naturalised through symbolic violence, so identity is shaped as much by how others classify migrants as by migrants themselves."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): a Paper 2 practice introduction written for this question bank.

Explain why this introduction is likely to lead to a strong Paper 2 answer, using one or more anthropological concepts. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: It contextualises the ethnography precisely, signals depth in one ethnography, introduces key concepts (identity, classification, power through symbolic violence) and sets up an argument that goes beyond description, so the essay can be analytical and focused.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: It contextualises the ethnography precisely, signals depth in one ethnography, introduces key concepts (identity, classification, power through symbolic violence) and sets up an argument that goes beyond description, so the essay can be analytical and focused. Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Outline one way in which using Carsten for a question on social organisation shows linking ethnography to an area of inquiry.
items.answer: Carsten shows Langkawi villagers becoming kin by eating rice from the same hearth and fostering children. Detailed evidence of feeding and co-residence supports an argument that kinship is a process, linking to the concept of social relations.
items.markingKey: Context (Carsten shows Langkawi villagers becoming kin by eating rice from the same hearth and fostering children.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: detailed evidence of feeding and co-residence supports an argument that kinship is a process, linking to the concept of social relations. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to linking ethnography to an area of inquiry.

items.stem: Explain how Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments illustrates the concept of power. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Women and young men – those with less power – express love, loss and vulnerability through short ghinnawa poems, a socially acceptable channel for sentiments that would breach the honour code if spoken directly.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Women and young men – those with less power – express love, loss and vulnerability through short ghinnawa poems, a socially acceptable channel for sentiments that would breach the honour code if spoken directly. Award up to [5]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Lila Abu-Lughod, Veiled Sentiments: Honor and Poetry in a Bedouin Society (1986), among the Awlad 'Ali Bedouin of Egypt's Western Desert (fieldwork from 1978)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: An answer about Holmes's work could also consider ethical issues such as his illegal border crossing and representing undocumented workers, which the student might mention when evaluating methods. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

Read the text below.

Draft introduction by a student: "In this essay I will discuss how migration changes identity. With reference to identity, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments. Your answer should identify both similarities and differences.
items.answer: Text: It contextualises the ethnography precisely, signals depth in one ethnography, introduces key concepts (identity, classification, power through symbolic violence) and sets up an argument that goes beyond description, so the essay can be analytical and focused. Ethnography – Lila Abu-Lughod, Veiled Sentiments: Honor and Poetry in a Bedouin Society (1986), among the Awlad 'Ali Bedouin of Egypt's Western Desert (fieldwork from 1978): Honour and modesty (hasham) define ideal personhood; in public people present themselves as autonomous and invulnerable, especially before those of higher status. Comparison: similarities and differences in how identity is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Text: It contextualises the ethnography precisely, signals depth in one ethnography, introduces key concepts (identity, classification, power through symbolic violence) and sets up an argument that goes beyond description, so the essay can be analytical and focused. Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: In a Paper 2 essay, what most distinguishes a top-band answer from a middle-band answer?
options: Use of many ethnographies briefly
Quoting the question repeatedly
Length
Critical use of detailed ethnography and key concepts to build a sustained argument
items.answer: Critical use of detailed ethnography and key concepts to build a sustained argument
items.markingKey: D. Depth, accuracy and analysis are rewarded.

items.stem: Explain why critical engagement with an ethnography strengthens a Paper 2 answer.
items.answer: Evaluating the ethnographer's methods, positionality and theory shows understanding that ethnographic knowledge is constructed and allows a more balanced, convincing argument.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Evaluating the ethnographer's methods, positionality and theory shows understanding that ethnographic knowledge is constructed and allows a more balanced, convincing argument. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between analysing an ethnography and summarising an ethnography.
items.answer: Summarising retells what the ethnography contains; analysing explains how its evidence and argument answer the question, using concepts and theory.
items.markingKey: Summarising retells what the ethnography contains; analysing explains how its evidence and argument answer the question, using concepts and theory. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Knowledge of the ethnographer's methods is as important as knowledge of the findings." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Methods matter to evaluate evidence, but should be used in the service of answering the question.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: methods shape the evidence; evaluation of methods strengthens critical engagement. Arguments against: questions focus on concepts and areas of inquiry; too much on methods can drift from the question. Supported judgement: Methods matter to evaluate evidence, but should be used in the service of answering the question. Markbands (15 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evaluation"?
options: Combining insights from both ethnographies to reach a conclusion that neither alone supports
The verb in a question (e.g. evaluate, discuss, to what extent) that specifies the kind of thinking required
The IB marking principle of placing a response in the band whose descriptor it matches most closely overall
Weighing the strengths and limitations of ethnographies and arguments to reach a supported judgement
items.answer: Weighing the strengths and limitations of ethnographies and arguments to reach a supported judgement
items.markingKey: D. "evaluation" is weighing the strengths and limitations of ethnographies and arguments to reach a supported judgement.

items.stem: "A comparison only needs to show that two ethnographies are about the same topic." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A comparison must explain specific similarities and differences relevant to the question and analyse why they arise.
items.markingKey: A comparison must explain specific similarities and differences relevant to the question and analyse why they arise. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between similarity of findings and similarity of method.
items.answer: Similar findings mean the ethnographies reach comparable conclusions; similar methods mean they used comparable research techniques. Both should be considered.
items.markingKey: Similar findings mean the ethnographies reach comparable conclusions; similar methods mean they used comparable research techniques. Both should be considered. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to comparing Scott and Ong on resistance, explain how it illustrates comparing two ethnographies through theory.
items.answer: Scott's Malay peasants used gossip and foot-dragging; Ong's Malay factory women experienced spirit possession on the shop floor. Both fit the theory of everyday resistance, but differ in gender, setting (village/factory) and idiom (moral gossip/spirits), showing how culture shapes resistance.
items.markingKey: Context (Scott's Malay peasants used gossip and foot-dragging; Ong's Malay factory women experienced spirit possession on the shop floor.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: both fit the theory of everyday resistance, but differ in gender, setting (village/factory) and idiom (moral gossip/spirits), showing how culture shapes resistance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to comparing two ethnographies through theory.

Two paragraphs from a student essay: "Bourgois (1995) argues that crack dealers in East Harlem build a street culture of resistance in search of respect. Holmes (2013) argues that Triqui pickers in Washington are placed in an ethnic-citizenship hierarchy. Both are about poor Latinos in the USA." Using evidence from the text, describe the student's two paragraphs and the teacher's comment. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.
items.answer: The student summarises Bourgois's argument about street culture and respect and Holmes's argument about the ethnic-citizenship hierarchy, and notes both are about poor Latinos in the USA; the teacher criticises the lack of comparison, connecting concept and attention to methods.
items.markingKey: The student summarises Bourgois's argument about street culture and respect and Holmes's argument about the ethnic-citizenship hierarchy, and notes both are about poor Latinos in the USA; the teacher criticises the lack of comparison, connecting concept and attention to methods. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Using Malkki's Purity and Exile (among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)) as your example, describe how power is shown.
items.answer: Camp administration regulated movement and livelihoods, and refugees' narratives of persecution were also a response to their marginal position.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Camp administration regulated movement and livelihoods, and refugees' narratives of persecution were also a response to their marginal position. Award up to [5]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Liisa Malkki, Purity and Exile: Violence, Memory, and National Cosmology among Hutu Refugees in Tanzania (1995), among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Theory is more important than ethnographic detail in a Paper 2 comparison."
items.answer: Both are needed: theory interprets, detail supports; top answers integrate them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: theory explains patterns; it shows conceptual understanding. Arguments against: without detail, theory is unsupported assertion; markbands reward detailed, accurate ethnography. Supported judgement: Both are needed: theory interprets, detail supports; top answers integrate them.

synthesis
markband
essay plan
items.answer: point-by-point structure
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of point-by-point structure.

items.stem: Explain why choosing contrasting ethnographies can produce stronger essays.
items.answer: Contrasts in setting, scale or theory reveal how context shapes a concept, allowing more insightful analysis than comparing very similar cases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Contrasts in setting, scale or theory reveal how context shapes a concept, allowing more insightful analysis than comparing very similar cases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Elena writes: "Theory should be kept separate from ethnographic evidence." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Strong answers integrate theory and evidence, using theory to interpret ethnography and ethnography to test theory.
items.markingKey: Strong answers integrate theory and evidence, using theory to interpret ethnography and ethnography to test theory. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe comparing Malkki and Levitt on belonging and explain what it reveals about comparing belonging under forced and voluntary movement.
items.answer: Malkki's refugees narrate exile and a homeland of return; Levitt's Dominican migrants live transnationally between Boston and Miraflores. Both show belonging oriented towards a place of origin, but forced displacement produces a moral narrative of exile while labour migration produces practical transnational ties.
items.markingKey: Context (Malkki's refugees narrate exile and a homeland of return; Levitt's Dominican migrants live transnationally between Boston and Miraflores.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: both show belonging oriented towards a place of origin, but forced displacement produces a moral narrative of exile while labour migration produces practical transnational ties. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to comparing belonging under forced and voluntary movement.

items.stem: Which use of planning time is most effective for a Paper 2 essay?
items.answer: Writing a thesis and choosing specific ethnographic evidence for each point
items.markingKey: Writing a thesis and choosing specific ethnographic evidence for each point. A focused plan supports a coherent argument.

items.stem: Distinguish between "discuss" and "evaluate".
items.answer: "Evaluate" requires an appraisal weighing strengths and limitations; "discuss" requires a balanced review of a range of arguments. Both need a supported conclusion.
items.markingKey: "Evaluate" requires an appraisal weighing strengths and limitations; "discuss" requires a balanced review of a range of arguments. Both need a supported conclusion. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify one way in which power matters in Farmer's AIDS and Accusation (in Do Kay, a village in rural central Haiti settled by people displaced by the Péligre hydroelectric dam) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Farmer argues that HIV spread in Haiti along lines of structural violence – poverty, loss of land to the Péligre dam, gender inequality and US economic dominance – not because of "risky culture".
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Farmer argues that HIV spread in Haiti along lines of structural violence – poverty, loss of land to the Péligre dam, gender inequality and US economic dominance – not because of "risky culture". Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Paul Farmer, AIDS and Accusation: Haiti and the Geography of Blame (1992), in Do Kay, a village in rural central Haiti settled by people displaced by the Péligre hydroelectric dam); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Using Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline and Farmer's AIDS and Accusation, compare the ways in which space, place and time is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline (among young Malay women working in Japanese-owned electronics factories in Kuala Langat, Selangor, Malaysia (late 1970s)): Factories imposed clock time and spatial control – bounded workstations, microscopes, supervisors – that clashed with the rhythms of village life. Farmer's AIDS and Accusation (in Do Kay, a village in rural central Haiti settled by people displaced by the Péligre hydroelectric dam): A "geography of blame" linked Haiti and the United States: the epidemic moved along routes of migration, tourism and economic dependence, yet blame flowed towards the poorer country. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far space, place and time is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Explain why candidates should self-assess using markbands.
items.answer: Matching one's answer to band descriptors shows what distinguishes higher bands – depth, analysis, evaluation – and gives precise targets for improvement.

items.stem: A student claims: "Writing more always earns more marks in Paper 2." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Marks depend on quality – focus, accuracy, analysis and evaluation – not length.

items.stem: Distinguish between similarity of method and similarity of findings.

items.stem: Distinguish between a block comparison and a point-by-point comparison.

Compare and contrast the role of power in the text with power in one ethnography you have studied, such as Bourgois's In Search of Respect. Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: Link both through a concept such as structural and symbolic violence; compare explicitly: both trace suffering to structural forces, but Bourgois's dealers resist through an oppositional culture while Holmes's pickers partly accept their position (symbolic violence); contrast settings (urban drug economy vs agricultural labour) and methods (Bourgois living in the neighbourhood, Holmes working as a picker and crossing the border). Ethnography – Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

Ethnography – Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. items.stem: Compare and contrast how belonging is shown in Peggy Levitt, The Transnational Villagers (2001) and Liisa Malkki, Purity and Exile: Violence, Memory, and National Cosmology among Hutu Refugees in Tanzania (1995).
items.answer: Levitt's The Transnational Villagers (among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston): Migrants belonged to two places at once, joining village development and politics from Boston. Malkki's Purity and Exile (among Hutu refugees from Burundi who fled the 1972 killings, in Mishamo refugee camp and Kigoma township, Tanzania (fieldwork 1985–1986)): Camp refugees saw exile as a moral trial and Burundi as the homeland to which they truly belonged; town refugees sought to belong locally. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far belonging is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Big question: "Is there such a thing as a universal human experience?" Discuss with reference to the key concept of social relations and at least one ethnography you have studied, such as Carsten's The Heat of the Hearth.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies social relations explicitly and uses ethnography: Kinship is created by living together and sharing food, especially rice cooked on the same hearth, so people become kin through feeding and co-residence, not only through birth. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
